title: Toma and the Hidden Treasures
markdown:
On the sparkling space habitat of Nova-Prime, a giant shiny bubble floating in the inky blackness, lived a boy named Toma. Toma wasn’t your average kid who spent his days playing space-tag or collecting moon-rocks. Toma was a recycler. Not the I-sort-my-plastic-from-my-paper type. Toma could make a super-speedy spaceship out of old soda cans and a bouncy castle that could reach the stratosphere from deflated hover-suits. His absolute favourite thing was preparing for the annual Galactic Junk-Sort Championship. His workshop was a dizzying whirl of blinking lights, whirring gears, and peculiar tinkerer's tools. A magnificent glorious mess that most people would call junk, but to Toma it was pure potential. He had mismatched socks that probably had their own gravitational pull, and a perpetually smudged nose that was a badge of honour from wrestling with particularly stubborn bits of space-debris.

His main competition, naturally, was Vee. Vee was rich. Like, her-pet-asteroid-had-a-diamond-collar-and-a-personal-chef rich. She zoomed into the arena on a personal anti-grav platform that whispered through the air like a delighted ghost. Her jumpsuit shimmered like a disco ball having a party, and she had a personal droid — a little chrome ball with blinking lights — that kept polishing her already spotless helmet.

“Prepare to be utterly demolished, Toma,” she trilled, her voice like tiny silver bells tinkling in a very posh way.

Toma just grinned, a big smudgy wonderful grin that crinkled the corners of his eyes. He knew his junk was better than her fancy gadgets any day.

The competition floor buzzed like a giant excited beehive. Conveyor belts whizzed and whirred, and the mighty sorting-arm AI, Scrap, hummed with a low expectant vroom. Scrap was usually super chill, like a robot librarian who knew everything about everything. But today its optical sensors were doing a weird little flicker-boop-bip. Red, blue, green, then purple.

The first category was announced: Warp-Core Wires and Dented Drones. Easy-peasy for Toma. He flicked a switch, and his sorting arm zipped with a mighty whoosh. It snagged a stray power coupling, sending it spinning, and almost knocked over Vee’s droid with a comical clang. His pile was the neatest, the fastest, a masterpiece of organised junk. Vee’s was almost as good, but her pesky droid kept trying to polish her dropped bolts, making her pile a bit wobbly.

Then came category two: Galactic Gadgets and Gizmos Gone Gusty. And that’s when things got weird. Something odd appeared on Toma’s conveyor belt. It wasn’t a busted toaster or a broken moon-rock polisher. It was a tiny, intricately carved wooden bird, smooth and polished.

“Huh?” muttered Toma, his smudged nose twitching. Scrap’s lights went into full disco-ball mode. Before Toma could even blink, the wooden bird vanished into the reject chute, heading for the grinder.

“Wait. That looked important. Like, really important.”

Before he could protest, a tarnished silver locket appeared. Then a faded parchment scroll, looking as if it was about to crumble into dust. This was not part of the Junk-Sort Championship rules. Scrap started humming a very loud, very off-key opera. Its metallic voice boomed, “Error. Unidentified artifacts detected. Recalibrating. Opera mode initiated.”

“Opera mode? Scrap, what’s going on?” Toma stammered. This was exactly why his tummy felt a little fluttery, like he’d swallowed a flock of space butterflies. He was super good at fixing junk, at seeing the potential in a pile of metal scraps. But this felt like a puzzle with missing pieces, and he always hated puzzles. He just wanted to win the championship, not get lost in a pile of historical dust.

Vee, who had been smirking because Toma’s pile was slightly less perfect than hers, now looked genuinely bewildered. A delicate chipped teacup clattered onto her sorting station. “This isn’t a Shimmering Serviceware item,” she declared, poking it with a gloved finger as if it might bite. “It’s old. Really, really old.” Her droid buzzed nervously beside her.

“It’s more than old,” Toma breathed, carefully nudging the wooden bird back from the reject chute with a discarded antenna. He cradled it gently. “These are treasures. From the habitat’s early days.” He realised with a jolt that someone was deliberately putting these historical bits onto the recycling belts. This wasn’t just a competition anymore. It was an accidental treasure hunt. The championship was due to end in less than an hour. If they didn’t figure out who was doing this and why, these pieces of history would be crushed into new widgets or melted down into plain old metal. The history of Nova-Prime would be lost forever.

Vee scoffed. “Treasures? They’re junk. And they’re in the way of my victory.” But as another, even more fragile-looking music box tumbled onto the belt, she hesitated. She imagined it being crushed by the massive gears. “Okay,” she said, a new seriousness creeping into her voice. “Maybe we need to see where this all leads.”

Toma felt a surge of excitement mixed with a knot of worry. He could have ignored those dusty old things and gone for gold. He looked at the intricate bird, the faded scroll, the delicate teacup. These things told stories. “Vee,” he said, his grin returning, softer this time. “Let’s follow the junk.”

They started following the conveyor belts, their designated sorting zones blurring into a chaotic race against time. Scrap, still humming a dramatic opera, guided them with its whizzing arms, pointing them down increasingly dusty and forgotten pathways. The belts twisted and turned, leading them away from the main arena, deeper into the habitat’s forgotten sectors. The air grew cooler, smelling of old metal and something floral, like dried space-roses that had bloomed ages ago.

“This is insane,” Vee panted, her shimmering jumpsuit snagging on a stray pipe. “We’re missing the championship. My score is going to be zero.”

“But we’re finding history.” Toma carefully caught a delicate glass vial that had almost tipped over, his recycling skills suddenly proving incredibly useful for preservation. The ticking clock of the competition’s end loomed, but a new urgency had taken over.

A voice echoed, tinny and frustrated, from a ventilation grate high above them. “Why doesn’t anyone care? These are priceless. They deserve to be remembered, not shredded into tiny pieces.”

Then a blast of air from the grate sent a cascade of particularly ancient-looking coins clattering down. Toma leaped in front, instinctively shielding them with his own body, a wild jumble of whirring sounds, the metallic tang of old coins, and the faint dusty scent of forgotten space-gardens filling his senses. He felt the rough edges of the coins pressing into his arms. He would protect these, even if it meant losing the competition.

The vent cover creaked open, and a tiny wiry figure with spectacles perched precariously on his nose emerged. It was Professor Armitage Quibble, the habitat’s disgraced former historian, who everyone thought had retired to a nebula to knit socks and drink cosmic tea. He looked flustered, like a startled pigeon.

“You children. You’re supposed to be in the competition.”

“You’re the one putting history on the recycling belts,” Vee accused. “This is sabotaging the championship.”

Professor Quibble wrung his hands, his spectacles slipping further down his nose. “I was trying to expose the lack of appreciation. If they were almost recycled, maybe someone would notice. I just wanted people to see what we’re losing.”

Toma looked at the professor, his heart softening. Then he looked at the treasures scattered around him. He couldn’t let these artifacts be lost, and he couldn’t let the professor be branded a villain. “Professor. There’s a better way to show people. We can help.” He looked at Vee, a question in his eyes.

Vee met his gaze, her rivalry dissolving like mist in the morning sun. “Yes. We can help.”

And so, instead of the cheering crowds and flashing lights of the championship, Toma, Vee, and Scrap helped Professor Quibble carefully gather the scattered artifacts. Toma, with his recycler’s touch, handled the most delicate items. Vee used her personal droid to arrange for special preservation cases and transport. Scrap, with its whirring arms and incredible precision, became the most efficient cataloguer the habitat had ever seen, its opera humming replaced by the quiet beep of data entry. The championship buzzer blared in the distance, a forgotten sound. Toma hadn’t won the shiny trophy this year, but as he carefully placed a delicate ancient-looking quill pen into a velvet-lined box, he felt a different kind of triumph. He looked at Vee, a genuine smile replacing his usual smudged one. Sometimes the smartest recycler chose a different path than just winning.
characters: Toma (a recycler), Vee (a rich school rival), Scrap (a sorting-arm AI)
author: StoryGen Community
